topic: The Binary Secret of the Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students and introductory Computer Science students

sections.title: The Legend and the Rules
lecture_lines: Legend says monks move sixty-four disks between three pillars.
Only one disk moves at a time.
Larger disks cannot sit on smaller ones.
animations: Draw three gray pillars (#808080) on a black background. Place a stack of three disks (Red #FF0000, Green #00FF00, Blue #0000FF) on the leftmost pillar.
Move the smallest Red disk (#FF0000) from the first pillar to the second pillar using a smooth arc.
Try to move the largest Blue disk (#0000FF) from the first pillar onto the Red disk on the second pillar. Show a red "X" (#FF0000) over the move and return the Blue disk to the first pillar.
Highlight all three pillars and the stack with a soft white glow (#FFFFFF) to emphasize the puzzle setup.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Counter
lecture_lines: Binary counting uses only zeros and ones.
In three bits, we count from zero to seven.
Notice how each bit toggles at a specific frequency.
animations: Display the text '000' in the center with a light blue color (#ADD8E6).
Replace the digits with three circles. Initially, all are dark gray (#555555).
Animate the circles toggling between dark gray (#555555) and bright yellow (#FFFF00) as the counter increments from 001 to 111, with the corresponding binary string displayed above.

sections.title: The Mapping: Disks as Bits
lecture_lines: Every disk corresponds to a specific binary bit.
Disk one is the rightmost, least significant bit.
Moving n disks requires two to the n minus one moves.
The current move number identifies which disk to move.
Watch as move numbers map to specific disks.
animations: Display the formula 'Total Moves = 2^n - 1' in a bold white font (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
Show three disks stacked vertically. Label them from top to bottom: 'Disk 1', 'Disk 2', 'Disk 3' in light green (#90EE90).
Add a mapping label next to each disk: 'Disk 1 -> Bit 0', 'Disk 2 -> Bit 1', 'Disk 3 -> Bit 2' in a contrasting cyan (#00FFFF).

sections.title: The Rule of the Rightmost Set Bit
lecture_lines: To find the disk, write the move number in binary.
Find the position of the rightmost digit one.
Position one means move the smallest disk.
Position two means move the second smallest disk.
This pattern holds for every move in the puzzle.
animations: Show the decimal number '4' and its binary equivalent '100' in large white text (#FFFFFF).
Underline the '1' in '100' with a gold color (#FFD700) and display the text 'Rightmost 1 at position 3' below it.
Show an arrow pointing from the gold '1' to a graphic of 'Disk 3' (#1E90FF) to indicate it is the disk to move.

sections.title: Animated Walkthrough: 3-Disk Demo
lecture_lines: Move one is binary zero-zero-one; move disk one.
Move two is zero-one-zero; move disk two.
Move three is zero-one-one; move disk one again.
Move four is one-zero-zero; move disk three.
Binary counting guides every single disk placement perfectly.
animations: Display 'Step 1: 001' on the left and move Disk 1 (#FF6347) from Peg 1 to Peg 3 on the right.
Display 'Step 2: 010' and move Disk 2 (#32CD32) from Peg 1 to Peg 2.
Display 'Step 3: 011' and move Disk 1 (#FF6347) from Peg 3 to Peg 2.
Display 'Step 4: 100' and move Disk 3 (#1E90FF) from Peg 1 to Peg 3.
Display 'Step 7: 111' and move the final Disk 1 (#FF6347) to Peg 3, completing the stack.

sections.title: Conclusion: Mathematical Elegance
lecture_lines: Binary logic transforms a complex puzzle into simple counting.
Computers use this efficiency to solve recursive problems.
The Tower of Hanoi hides a binary heartbeat.
animations: Create a 'Binary Bridge' visual using two horizontal lines (#B0C4DE) with binary digits (0, 1) floating between them.
Fade in a 3-disk Tower of Hanoi stack on the right side of the bridge and the formula '2^n - 1' on the left side.
Group all elements and scale them down while a final 'Mathematical Elegance' title (#FFFFFF) fades in at the center.
